newsitem.title: KUWAIT: FOCUS-Kuwait moving on $1.5bln aromatics project.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Kuwait moving on $1.5bln aromatics project.

text.p: Kuwait's Petrochemical Industries Company (PIC) will complete in late March a feasibility study for an armocatics project worth between $1 billion and $1.5 billion, PIC's deputy chairman said on Wednesday.
"We hope the plant could start production by 1999 or 2000," Abullatif al-Haddad told Reuters of the project which would be open to foreign participation.
Using Kuwaiti naphtha as feedstock, the plant would produce materials such as benzene, xylene and paraxylnene -- raw materials for textiles such as acrylic fibre.
PIC last year "stopped and did not cut" joint venture talks on the project with U.S. firm Amoco Corp and decided on the feasibility study to identify Kuwait's requirement.
"We did not reach agreement (with Amoco) and decided on a different path...We will decide (according to the study) on the kind of products, capacity and future expansion," Haddad said.

PIC, a subsidiary of the state-owned Kuwait Petroleum Corp (KPC), has not decided to carry out the project on its own and plans to offer it to foreign partners. PIC reported a 123.5 percent rise in 1995/96 (July-June) net profit to $133.5.

"We changed the approach: 'This is what we want, would you (international firms) like to form a partnership, please here it is'. If we do not find a partner and we find that the project is good, we will go ahead with it on our own," added Haddad.

PIC has already secured approval in principle for Kuwaiti private investors to take a 20 percent stake in the proposed project compared to a 10 percent share in the $2 billion Equate Petrochemicals Company which will start production in August.
PIC and America's Union Carbide each have 45 percent of Equate, which is chaired by Haddad, while the local Bubiyan Petrochemical Co has the remaining 10 percent.
National Bank of Kuwait (NBK) last year arranged a $1.2 billion loan for Equate in which a host of international and regional banks participated.

"Banks are already calling us now...regional, domestic and big international institutions to say if you want we are ready (to provide financing for the aromatics project). I think our success with Equate has encouraged banks," said Haddad.

Mechanical completion at Equate is due in July and the plant will start producing at 60 percent capacity by mid-August rising to 90 percent after two months. It has an annual production capacity of 650,000 tonnes of ethylene, 450,000 tonnes of polyethylene and 350,000 tonnes per year of ethylene glycol.

Kuwait, which has a two million barrel per day OPEC quota, is a latecomer to the petrochemical industry in an oil-rich region where neighbouring Saudi Arabia and other Gulf Arab states have spent billions of dollars in the past 15 years developing an advanced petrochemical industry.
"Kuwait was delayed a lot but it is not too late," said Haddad of ambitious plans to raise revenue from higher-value refined oil products and petrochemicals by using cheap power and feedstocks.
A wholly-owned, 100,000-tonne-a-year PIC polypropylene plant will start production in September.
PIC, which says Equate will be the Gulf region's largest polyethylene and ethylene glycol plants, is not expected to compete with output from regional giant Saudi Basic Industries Corp.
"There is big demand and there is place. The market can absorb us and absorb them (SABIC)," said Haddad.

"There is coordination with SABIC and they helped us...I do not think we will reach this stage of cutting each others prices because there is demand and if we do (reach that stage) we will coordinate with our brothers in Saudi Arabia," he added.
PIC and Union Carbide set up a 50-50 marketing company in Bahrain -- Equate Marketing -- to secure Asian export deals.
